newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Army reform inevitable, PM tells Russia top brass.
newsitem.headline: Army reform inevitable, PM tells Russia top brass.

text.p: Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin told Russia's top brass on Thursday that military reform will be painful but that drastic cuts are inevitable.
Chernomyrdin made his comments just hours after Defence Minister Igor Rodionov urged extreme measures to save the struggling armed forces from final collapse.

Earlier on Tuesday, Chernomyrdin discussed the subject in a telephone conversation with President Boris Yeltsin, who is successfully recovering in Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital after heart surgery a week ago.

Interfax news agency quoted Chernomyrdin saying at a meeting of senior officers that military reform should affect not only the armed forces proper but also troops controlled by other agencies, including the Interior and Emergencies ministries.
"We have to take decisive measures, including unpopular ones," he said "This is needed for maintaining the country's defence potential."
Earlier in the day Rodionov addressed a separate meeting of senior officers and said that Russia faced a catastrophe unless it took extreme measures to reform the military.
"The armed forces today have come to the point where a further reduction in their combat readiness could lead to unforeseeble, tragic consequences," Interfax quoted him saying.
"If extreme measures are not taken to reform the army in the near future, the consequences for the state could be catastrophic."

Rodionov's latter comment, shown in television footage shot by NTV commercial television, was a step up in his struggle to persuade the government to increase defence spending and pay soldiers who have not received their wages for months.
He has played down talk of a military rebellion but said repeatedly that the problems could soon get out of control unless defence spending is increased.
Delays in paying army wages have caused serious discontent since Yeltsin's re-election in July. The government has struggled to meet its payments obligations against a background of low tax receipts.

Rodionov's gloomy message increased the pressure on the government to meet its spending obligations while simultaneously trying to boost its tax revenues to satisfy the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended loan payments to Moscow.
Finance Minister Alexander Livshits said on Tuesday that talks with the Fund on paying out a new tranche of Russia's $10 billion three-year loan were difficult.
"The results of the talks will be clear in about 10 days. The talks are definitely difficult. Definitely difficult," Livshits told reporters.

An IMF mission left Moscow last month after regular monitoring of Russia's economic performance but postponed a decision on whether the tranche should be paid out, saying that poor tax collection was threatening fiscal policy.
Many of the government's problems have been aggravated by Yeltsin's long absence from work, and he is still unlikely to return to return to his Kremlin office for another two months.

The presidential press service issued a statement saying a council of doctors had examined Yeltsin on Tuesday, exactly a week after his quintuple heart bypass, and concluded that the 65-year-old leader was in a "completely satisfactory" condition.
He is being allowed to move around more and more. His pulse and blood pressure are stable, his temperature is normal and there are no complications with his blood, it said.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin planned to broadcast to the nation in the next few days.
Yastrzhembsky said the Russian leader spoke by telephone on Tuesday with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl, who advised him not to force the pace of his return to work.

Yastrzhembsky said Kohl had renewed an invitation to the 65-year-old Kremlin chief to convalesce in Germany. Yeltsin, who underwent a quintuple heart bypass operation, told Kohl he needed time to think over the invitation.
